solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Nasty girl not right about a single complaint

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes around the other
something not right is out of order or deranged, so these letters must be rearranged

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter as the fodder
I is the Roman numeral one, a single unit

explanation.surface: A spiteful young woman, rather unhinged, is griping about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nasty' looks like the adjective doing the work, but it is part of the letters to be shuffled; 'not right' does the shuffling. The anagram becomes LARYNG...TIS and I slots in to give LARYNGITIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in British usage is an illness or ailment, and inflammation of the voice box is one such medical condition.

clue.text: What might irritate some smaller gentlemen

indicators.note: 'some' asks for only a portion, so the letters sit as a run inside the following words

parts.note: the run starts after the opening letters of the first word and ends partway into the second

explanation.surface: A wry suggestion that shorter men can be a source of annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the word break: sm-ALLER GEN-tlemen.
explanation.definitionFit: Any substance such as pollen or dust that provokes a bodily reaction like sneezing or itching qualifies, so it is something that may irritate.

clue.text: Evergreen character on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio we only hear things, so the letters come from what is heard rather than what is written

parts.note: a character is a letter of the alphabet; this one is the twenty-first

explanation.surface: A long-running figure on a radio show who never goes away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evergreen character' reads like a long-serving soap role; split it, and the character is the letter U, said aloud as the tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The tree keeps its dark needles all year round, so it is a classic example of an evergreen conifer.

clue.text: Birds my sage stuffing is not used in

parts.note: 'my!' and 'gee!' are both exclamations of surprise

indicators.note: the stuffing is the filling, and leaving it out keeps only the outside of the word

parts.note: the herb with its middle two letters removed

explanation.surface: A cook prepares roast birds but leaves out the usual sage stuffing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'my' is not a possessive here but the exclamation, the same as GEE. Sage-and-onion stuffing is a traditional filling for a roast goose, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: These large waterfowl are birds, the plural of goose, often roasted for a festive meal.

clue.text: Nuclear accord chief whip initially switched

indicators.note: switching the initial letters of two words is exactly what the Reverend Spooner famously did

parts.note: the chief one is the BEST; it keeps its body but takes the opening letter of its partner
to whip someone is to TAN their hide; it hands its opening letter over and takes the other's

explanation.surface: A nuclear treaty is suddenly changed by a party's chief whip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chief whip' looks like the parliamentary officer, but the two words are clued separately; swap the first letters of BEST TAN and you get TEST BAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A treaty forbidding the trial detonation of atomic weapons, such as the 1963 one, is an international agreement of this nuclear kind.

clue.text: Biology classes sure began badly

indicators.note: something done badly comes out wrong, so the letters end up in a jumbled order

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A school's biology lessons certainly got off to a poor start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classes' suggests school lessons, but here it means categories in biological classification.
explanation.definitionFit: In taxonomy a genus can be split into smaller ranks, and those ranks are categories or classes used by biologists.

clue.text: A creature that's immature in more ways than one

definitions.text: A creature that's immature in more ways than one

parts.note: a young dog or seal is a juvenile animal
taken as written

explanation.surface: An animal that is childish in several respects.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a young animal followed by A, and also an insect in its undeveloped stage. 'in more ways than one' flags the double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: An insect between larva and adult stages is not yet fully developed, so it is an immature creature.

clue.text: A dog entering overturned head boy's side dish

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one piece is placed within another
turned over in a down clue means flipped end to end, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the head of something is its top
a lad is a boy
taken as written
the tosa is a large Japanese fighting breed

explanation.surface: A dog knocks over the head boy's plate of salad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head boy' looks like a school title, but only 'head' is flipped. The tosa, a big Japanese breed, is a dog crosswords love because few solvers know it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold boiled potatoes in mayonnaise are served alongside a main course, making them an accompaniment on the plate.

clue.text: Looked annoyed when called out

indicators.note: calling something out means saying it aloud, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: piqued means irritated or resentful

explanation.surface: Someone appeared cross after being summoned or criticised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looked annoyed' reads as a single phrase, but 'Looked' is the definition and 'annoyed' supplies the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: To peek is to glance quickly or furtively, so the past tense is a type of having looked.

clue.text: Pure fluorine, unregulated

parts.note: F is the chemical symbol for fluorine
without laws or controls

explanation.surface: An advert for uncontrolled, undiluted fluorine gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pure fluorine' reads as one chemistry phrase; split it, and 'Pure' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without any blemish or defect is perfect and unspoilt, the sense of pure here.

clue.text: Who would place Yankees top?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a gambler; a Yankee is a British bookmakers' wager of eleven bets on four horses
second meaning: as a verb, to beat or surpass

explanation.surface: A question about who would rank the New York baseball team first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yankees' points at American baseball, but a Yankee is a type of multiple bet on horse races in Britain; 'top' is a verb disguised as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: One who wagers money is a gambler of this name, and to outdo or improve upon something is the verb sense matching top.

clue.text: Hearts captured by author convulse in pain

indicators.note: whatever is captured is held inside its captor, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: to author a book is to compose it, a verb here
H is the card-game abbreviation for the hearts suit

explanation.surface: A novelist seizes the affections of readers, who twist in agony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'author' looks like a noun, a writer, but it works as the verb; H goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To twist and squirm, as the body does when in agony, is the sense of convulsing in pain.

clue.text: One connected people in exchange for a living

definitions.text: One connected people in exchange for a living

parts.note: surface reading: someone who networked or traded for money
setter's reading: a switchboard centre, where calls were joined by hand

explanation.walkthrough: 'exchange' suggests trading or bartering, but it is the building where operators patched calls through.
explanation.definitionFit: Switchboard operators at a central office plugged in cables so that callers could talk, which was their paid work.

clue.text: Leader in being stern inspires the rest

indicators.note: the leader is whoever goes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece is drawn inside another

parts.note: the stern is the rear of a ship
taken as written

explanation.surface: A strict leader motivates the others in the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stern' looks like an adjective meaning strict, but it is the back of a boat, and 'inspires' is used in its literal sense of breathing in.
explanation.definitionFit: A short pause to catch one's breath is a break from effort, so it is a rest.

clue.text: Shaky performers leaving corporations exposed

parts.note: surface reading: unreliable artistes walking out and leaving businesses vulnerable
setter's reading: a corporation is old slang for a paunch, so these performers shimmy with midriffs bare

explanation.walkthrough: 'corporations' looks like big companies, but it is a jocular word for a stomach, and 'shaky' is literal: these dancers shake.
explanation.definitionFit: Dancers in the Middle Eastern style wear costumes baring the midriff and shake their hips, so they are performers who shimmy.

clue.text: A deb's told to get permed locks

indicators.note: a perm twists hair into new curls, so these letters are twisted into a new arrangement

parts.note: all three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A debutante is instructed to have her hair curled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locks' sits next to 'permed' to suggest hair, but it means door fastenings. A deb is a debutante, a young upper-class woman entering society.
explanation.definitionFit: These are bolts on doors moved by a key rather than a spring, so they are a sturdy kind of security fastening.

clue.text: Last on track are twin high jumpers

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

indicators.note: high can mean intoxicated, and anything intoxicated is in a muddled state

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Two high-jump athletes finish last on the athletics track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high jumpers' reads as one athletics phrase, but 'high' is the anagram signal. A jumper is British for a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: Knitted garments such as sweaters make up this category of clothing, so jumpers are an example of it.

clue.text: Aussie crook on prairies makes easy progress

parts.note: prairies are flat grassland, plains
in Australian slang 'crook' means ill or sick

explanation.surface: An Australian criminal on the run across the American grasslands gets on easily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crook' looks like a criminal, but in Australia it means unwell. 'on' places one piece after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes smooth progress with no obstacles, as a boat moves on calm waters, so it means easy going.

clue.text: Bulge after feeling one needed to eat like a horse

definitions.text: one needed to eat like a horse

indicators.note: 'after' places the piece it follows second, so the order of the clue is flipped in the answer

parts.note: a nose for something is an instinctive feeling for it
to bag is to bulge or sag, as trousers do at the knee

explanation.surface: A glutton notices a swelling waistline after eating huge amounts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eat like a horse' is the idiom for eating hugely, but here it is literal: a horse eats from this.
explanation.definitionFit: A feed bag hung over a horse's head holds its oats, so it is what an animal of that kind eats from.

clue.text: Extreme, almost cut off

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to cut off a limb is to sever it; the past participle loses its final D

explanation.surface: Being nearly amputated is drastic indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut off' gives SEVERED, and 'almost' trims the final D.
explanation.definitionFit: Very harsh or intense conditions, such as bitter weather or grave injury, are the sense of extreme here.

clue.text: Suspects put by soldiers in strongholds

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army
to suspect is to doubt, a verb

explanation.surface: Suspected criminals are detained by troops inside fortresses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspects' looks like a noun, people under suspicion, but it is the verb, mistrusts; the soldiers come first.
explanation.definitionFit: A redoubt is a small fortified outpost or defensive position, so it is a type of fortress or stronghold.

clue.text: Relaxed on a chair after daughter moved over

indicators.note: moving over means hopping across neighbours, so the letter lands back inside the word further along
something moved is taken from where it was, so that letter leaves its spot

parts.note: sitting on a chair means being seated
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Someone unwinds in an armchair once their daughter has gone off to another room.
explanation.walkthrough: The daughter is already in the seated word: no new letter arrives, the existing D just shifts two places earlier, past A and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A calm, unhurried, composed manner is the adjective sense, close in meaning to relaxed or placid.

clue.text: Fish tested for freshness?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small silvery food fish
second meaning: sniffed, as one checks milk to see whether it has gone off

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second meaning is an example rather than a dictionary synonym: you check freshness with your nose.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a little sea and river fish, and the British past tense of the verb meaning to sniff is spelt the same way.

clue.text: Golf, easy to excuse, but not very sociable

parts.note: Golf is G in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: 'not' says the following item is absent, so its letter is struck out

parts.note: a venial sin is a minor, pardonable one
V is the standard abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: Golf is easily forgiven, though it is not a particularly social game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not very sociable' reads as one unfriendly phrase, but 'not very' removes V and 'sociable' alone is the definition, the opposite of what the surface implies.
explanation.definitionFit: A warm, friendly and cheerful person is pleasant company, so the word is a synonym for affable or sociable.

clue.text: Clothing of a Cavalier king hiding in trees

indicators.note: whatever hides in something is concealed inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: beeches are broadleaf trees
R is for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A Royalist king hides in an oak tree, as Charles II famously did after Worcester.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cavalier king' suggests Charles, but the king is just R; 'Cavalier' belongs to the definition. Cavaliers were the Royalist side in the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: Knee-length trousers fastened below the knee were the standard legwear of seventeenth-century gentlemen, Royalists included.

clue.text: Signal that's pretty timeless

indicators.note: '-less' means without, so the word glued to it names a letter to be taken away

parts.note: pretty and cute are synonyms

explanation.surface: A sign or gesture that is lovely and never dates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'timeless' reads as one word meaning classic, but it splits into 'time' and 'less'.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's prompt to speak or enter is a sign or hint to act, so it is a signal.

clue.text: Animal on a farm without water

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old word for an ox or cow
second meaning: of spirits, served undiluted

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a parched farm, but the word is an archaic term for cattle and also how a whisky is ordered straight.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic English used the noun for cattle, and a drink served straight with nothing added is described by the same adjective.

clue.text: Tourists quote Burns as it is spoken

indicators.note: spoken words are heard rather than read, so the letters follow the sound

parts.note: to quote a source is to cite it
to burn meat on a hot pan is to sear it

explanation.surface: Visitors recite lines from Robert Burns in a Scots accent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burns' with its capital looks like the Scottish poet Robert Burns, but it is the verb; the capital is just camouflage.
explanation.definitionFit: Visitors who go around looking at famous places and landmarks are holidaymakers, so they are tourists.
